newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban sugar output set to continue bounceback.
newsitem.headline: Cuban sugar output set to continue bounceback.

text.p: Cuba, which has halted a five-year decline in its sugar production, will seek a further increase in the 1996-97 cane harvest due to start early next month, officials say.
It was not clear yet how far efforts may be hampered by very heavy rains that have hit most of the island for the last week and continued Monday in eastern areas of the country.
Flooding to small areas of sugar cane was reported in the eastern provinces of Holguin and Camaguey although flooded cane is usually recoverable if it is quickly drained.
Cuba raised sugar cane production to 4.45 million tonnes in the 1995-96 harvest from a low of 3.3 million tonnes in the 1994-95 crop.
No official target for 1996/97 has been published but sugar experts say the island is hoping for a crop of more than five million tonnes, probably around 5.2-5.3 million tonnes.

Sugar Minister Nelson Torres told state media at the weekend that cutting would start in December, with the eastern provinces of Santiago de Cuba and Granma the first to start. Authorities in Santiago de Cuba said the harvest there would start December 1.
By January most of the island's 156 mills would be operating, Torres said.
"The country is in a position to raise the harvest again," the minister said, but gave no target.
Holguin and Villa Clara, key producer provinces, should continue to increase output and produce more than 500,000 tonnes each, he said.
Some 3,000 harvesting machines and 80,000 hand cutters will be involved in the harvest, Torres added in an interview with the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina.

The minister did not mention damage to cane caused by Hurricane Lili, which swept central and western areas of the country on October 17-18. Although the storm flattened some cane and flooded other cane fields, authorities have said most of the affected cane will be useable for the harvest.

Alberto Betancourt, head of the state sugar trading company Cubazucar, told a sugar meeting in London earlier this month the hurricane had hit at a time when the cane was sufficiently mature to be able to withstand the storm. He added there was no doubt the 1996-97 harvest would show an improvement on last year.
Torres, referring to damage to sugar mills caused by the hurricane, such as broken roofs, said repairs would be carried out on time.
As in the 1995-96 harvest, Cuba has secured credits from foreign banks and trading houses for input to the sugar sector this year. However, officials have not said how much the credits were worth.
